approved: The speaker moved to introduce and present the Indigenous Education (Targeted Assistance) Amendment Bill (No. 2) 2013, which amends the Indigenous Education (Targeted Assistance) Act 2000, and the bill was read a first time.

The Minister for Indigenous Affairs tabled a bill to amend the Indigenous Education (Targeted Assistance) Act 2000, changing its funding mechanism from special to annual appropriation for greater transparency and allowing new funding agreements from 1 January 2014 to boost school attendance for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander students.

Introduced the Indigenous Education (Targeted Assistance) Amendment Bill (No. 2) 2013, which changes targeted Indigenous education funding from a special to an annual appropriation from 1 January 2014, following a 2013 to 2014 budget decision, to improve transparency and accountability.

Supported the bill, said the Commonwealth's Stronger Futures package funded 200 additional teachers and more than 100 teacher-housing units in the bush, but criticised the Northern Territory government for withdrawing $250 million from education over the forward estimates including $50 million next year, and said before 2001 no Aboriginal community in the Northern Territory had a school offering year 11 or 12.

Supported the bill, said 58 Indigenous students were enrolled in year 7 in Shepparton in 2010 but none remained by year 12, said 34.1 per cent of Indigenous people aged 15 and over reported year 9 or below as their highest level of schooling compared with 16 per cent of non-Indigenous people, and praised the 17-year-old Ganbina mentoring program for its outcomes despite ongoing gaps between teacher expectations and results.

Supported the bill, said the former Labor government invested more than $5.5 billion through the Closing the Gap framework since 2008, said the School Nutrition Program provided 2,972 breakfasts and 5,419 lunches daily to 67 Northern Territory schools between January and June 2013, and said year 3 Indigenous reading proficiency rose to 74.2 per cent in 2012 from 68.3 per cent in 2008, while numeracy proficiency fell to 72.7 per cent from 78.6 per cent over the same period.

Supported the bill for providing funding certainty to schools, citing a 2006 survey led by Fiona Stanley of 4,000 Aboriginal children and families in Western Australia that found a lack of continuity in program funding undermined educational attainment, and named Western Australian schools with large Aboriginal enrolments that would benefit from the change.

Supported the Indigenous Education (Targeted Assistance) Amendment Bill, highlighting Richardson Primary School's adult literacy program for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander parents and the Canberra-based Australian Indigenous Leadership Centre, whose graduates saw an average income increase of $13,877 after completing its courses.
